What the official sources say

  • The assessment rate is 20% of true, actual, or market value (Ark. Code Ann. 26-26-303(c)). (Arkansas Property Tax FAQs (DFA); source)
  • Market value is determined as of the January 1 valuation date of the tax year. (Arkansas Property Tax FAQs (DFA); source)
  • Taxes are due from the first business day in March through October 15 of the year following the assessment year; a 10% penalty applies if not paid by then. (Arkansas Property Tax FAQs (DFA); source)
  • Amendment 79 caps annual increases in taxable value after reappraisal at 5% for homesteads and 10% for other real property, until full assessed value is reached. (Property Tax Relief | DFA; source)
  • At least 30 calendar days before an in-person tax-delinquent auction, the Commissioner of State Lands notifies the owner and interested parties by regular mail of the right to redeem. (26 CAR 400-106; source)

How does the Arkansas property tax calendar work?

Arkansas runs property tax on a two-year cycle: values and millage rates are set in the assessment year, and the money is collected the following year. The Assessment Coordination Division of the state Department of Finance and Administration oversees all 75 counties, but assessing, collecting and distributing happens locally.

In the assessment year, county assessors, clerks, equalization boards and judges settle values. School boards, city councils and county quorum courts set millage, and the quorum court formally levies it. In the collection year, county clerks, collectors and treasurers bill, collect and pay out the money. Each assessment year is also the collection year for the one before it, so an owner is always dealing with two cycles at once.

Business personal property is assessed by May 31. The division's overview page lists the other dates that matter to a homeowner.

What millage rate will a house in Arkansas pay?

The state average across counties was 48.80 mills in the division's 2026 annual report, built from school, city and county rates after the 2025 school elections. The report breaks that down as 38.52 for schools, 4.17 for cities and 7.93 for counties.

Assessed value is 20% of market value, and the millage rate is applied to the assessed figure. The same report says school districts receive about 80% of property tax collections, counties about 15% and cities about 5%. Your own rate depends on the school district, the city and the county the house sits in, so two homes of the same value can get different bills.

The annual report is a long PDF, so use your county assessor's notice for the actual millage on your parcel.

How often is a home reappraised, and is there a cap?

Counties reappraise every four years under Act 139 of 2023, and by 2028 every county will be on a four-year contract. The annual report lists 19 counties reappraising in 2025 and 21 in 2026, with Baxter and Boone among those finishing in 2026.

Under Amendment 79, the taxable value of a homestead owned by someone under 65 who is not disabled can rise only 5% a year after a reappraisal. Other real property is capped at 10% a year. Credits for homesteads and the age 65 or disabled freeze are covered in our homestead guide, so this page stays on assessment and collection.

A cap limits how fast the taxable figure climbs. It does not stop the bill from rising when a school board raises millage.

What are the key dates for an Arkansas homeowner?

The dates below combine the state's published calendar with the Pulaski County Clerk's equalization timeline, which shows how one county applies them.

DateEvent
JulyAssessor mails notices of assessed value (Pulaski County)
August 1Equalization board holds its organizational meeting (Pulaski County)
Third Monday in AugustLast day to schedule a board hearing
September 30Regular board meetings end (Pulaski County)
Second Monday in OctoberLast day to petition county court
October 15Taxes due; unpaid bills turn delinquent
November 15County court must hear and rule on appeals
First business day of MarchCollection of the prior assessment year's bills begins

The Pulaski timeline also says no assessment can be changed after the board's special session ends in November. An owner who misses the August deadline should not count on a second chance that year.

How do you appeal an assessment?

You start with a talk with the county assessor, then take it to the county equalization board, then to county court, and then to circuit court. The appeal statute, 26-27-318, governs the county court step.

  • The board hears only the current year's value and cannot hear appeals of earlier years.
  • A county court petition is filed with the county clerk, who assigns a case number, and there is no filing fee.
  • You must have used the board first, unless you never received the required notice of a value change.
  • The county court publishes notice at least a week before the hearing, or it lacks jurisdiction.
  • You carry the burden to prove true value by a preponderance of the evidence, and no presumption favors the assessor.
  • The court's written decision must come within 20 working days after the hearing and must say you can go on to circuit court.

In the 2026 report, 598 properties had their values changed after informal appeals alone, which suggests the first conversation with the assessor is worth having. The statute does not state a circuit court deadline, so an owner heading there should ask an attorney.

What happens when Arkansas property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid taxes after October 15 are delinquent and carry a 10% penalty plus daily interest on real estate. The Craighead County Tax Collector's page lays this out, and says the collector publishes delinquent lists in a local newspaper.

The county does not hold a sale. Under Ark. Code 26-37-101, land still unpaid a year after the due date is certified to the Commissioner of State Lands by July 1 of the following year, and title vests in the state when certification arrives. Our tax deed guide walks through the steps after that.

For a seller, the practical point is that a delinquent bill is not a county matter you can quietly settle later. Once certification happens, the payoff goes through the state's office and the redemption deadline is firm.

When does the tax lien attach, and who pays at a sale?

The lien for property tax arises on the first Monday of January of the year of assessment and stays until the tax and penalties are paid. Section 26-34-101 gives it priority over judgments, executions, encumbrances and other liens, whenever those were created.

Between a grantor and a grantee, the statute delays the lien until the last date set by law for the county clerk to deliver the tax books to the collector. That timing is the reason the tax bill is a closing item and not just a seller's private matter.

Taxes are collected from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. A house sold in spring can therefore close while the prior year's bill is still unpaid. The title company can ask the collector for a status and pay what is owed from the seller's proceeds.

What should a seller check before listing with taxes due?

Confirm three things with the county: what is owed, what the next assessment will do, and whether any year is already delinquent.

  • Ask the collector for the current balance, with penalty and interest, by parcel number.
  • Read the latest assessor notice and note whether your county is reappraising this year.
  • If the August hearing date has passed, calendar the second Monday in October for county court.
  • If a year is delinquent, find out whether it has been certified to the Commissioner of State Lands.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses, including houses with back taxes. Bring your latest tax statement and assessor notice, and the title company can pay the collector at closing.

More questions about Arkansas Property Tax Guide

When is Arkansas property tax due?

Taxes are collected from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. A payment after October 15 draws a 10% penalty, and delinquent real estate accrues interest daily.

What is the deadline to challenge my assessment?

Schedule an equalization board hearing by the third Monday in August. If you disagree with the board, file a county court petition by the second Monday in October. The board cannot hear earlier years.

Does it cost anything to appeal to county court?

No filing fee applies to the petition of appeal under 26-27-318. You file with the county clerk, who assigns a case number, and the county court must rule by November 15.

How much can my homestead value rise in one year?

After a reappraisal, taxable value on a homestead owned by someone under 65 who is not disabled can rise 5% a year. Other real property is capped at 10% a year under Amendment 79.

Who sets my millage rate?

School boards, city councils and county quorum courts set it during the assessment year, and the quorum court formally levies it. The statewide county average was 48.80 mills in the 2026 annual report.

Does the tax lien follow the house to a new owner?

The lien binds the property and ranks ahead of other liens. In a transfer between grantor and grantee it does not attach until the clerk's tax-book delivery date, so confirm the balance with the collector before closing.

What the official sources say

  • Homeowners may receive a homestead property tax credit of up to $500 per year; beginning with 2026 tax bills the general assembly authorized an increase up to $600. (Property Tax Relief | DFA; source)
  • The homestead is the dwelling used as the principal place of residence; homeowners must apply for the credit with the county assessor's office. (Property Tax Relief | DFA; source)
  • A freeze does not pass to a subsequent owner of the same home; a buyer cannot claim the seller's prior limitation. (Property Tax Relief | DFA; source)
  • The October 15 deadline applies to filing the Homestead Credit Application. (Arkansas Assessment Coordination Division | DFA; source)
  • Property owners may claim only one homestead tax credit each year. (Property Tax Relief | DFA; source)

What is the Arkansas homestead tax credit worth now?

The credit is worth up to $675 a year on a qualifying home. The Assessment Coordination Division's 2026 annual report says it was raised from $600 by House Bill 1103 of 2026, and the Benton County and Washington County assessors both quote $675 on their public pages.

The state's property tax relief page still carries older wording, up to $500 and then up to $600 for 2026 tax bills. Treat the newer figure as the working number, and confirm it with your county assessor before you quote it to a buyer or a tax preparer.

The word exemption is common in everyday speech, but Arkansas gives a credit. Amendment 79, section 3, directs the General Assembly to provide an annual state credit against property tax on a homestead, and the credit cannot exceed the tax owed. The Benton County assessor gives an example: if the tax bill is $650, the credit pays $650 and nothing more, since the state does not send the difference.

Who qualifies, and where do you apply?

You qualify if the house is your principal place of residence and you hold the right kind of ownership interest. You apply with the county assessor's office where the house is located, as the Department of Finance and Administration states.

  • A record owner qualifies, and so does a buyer under a recorded sales contract or a person holding a recorded life estate.
  • The home may be held in a revocable or irrevocable trust.
  • A person who deeded the home away but kept a recorded life estate and still lives there can qualify.
  • A nursing home or retirement center resident who still owns the residence can qualify in some circumstances.
  • An LLC can qualify when it supplies a certificate of good standing and a member signs an attestation that the house is that member's primary residence and no other credit is claimed (Benton County assessor).

An owner may claim only one homestead credit per year. A landlord's rental house, a vacant inherited house and a second home do not meet the principal residence test.

Which Arkansas property tax breaks sit alongside the credit?

Amendment 79 produced three relief tools besides the credit: a freeze for owners 65 and older or disabled, a 5% yearly cap on homestead increases, and a 10% cap on other real property. The table sums them up.

BenefitWho gets itWhat it doesHow to get it
Homestead creditOwner-occupantsUp to $675 off the yearly tax billApply with the county assessor
Age 65 or disabled freezeHomestead owners who qualify for the creditFreezes the taxable assessed valueApply with the county assessor
Homestead capHomesteads after a reappraisalTaxable value rises 5% per year until it reaches full assessed valueApplied through the assessment
Cap on other real propertyCommercial, agricultural and vacant parcelsTaxable value rises 10% per year until full valueApplied through the assessment

The caps do not apply to newly discovered property, new construction or substantial improvements. Arkansas defines a substantial improvement as renovation, reconstruction and refurbishment that adds 25% or more to the value of the property.

Disabled veterans have a separate exemption. Act 407 of 2025 raised the contiguous land counted as the homestead for that exemption from 40 to 80 acres, effective for assessment years beginning on or after January 1, 2025.

How does the age 65 or disabled freeze work?

The freeze locks the taxable assessed value of the home at the next assessment date after you turn 65 or become disabled. It does not lock the tax bill. The Benton County assessor warns that a millage increase by a city, county or school district can still raise what you pay.

A person who is already 65 or disabled when buying a home can have the value frozen at the next assessment date after the purchase. The owner must apply, and the assessor asks for proof: a driver's license, state ID or birth certificate for age, or a Medicare card or Social Security award letter for disability, according to the Benton and Washington County pages.

Additions to the house can end the freeze. Benton County says the freeze is removed when a homeowner adds on and then reapplied at the new value.

What happens to the credit and the freeze when you sell?

Neither one travels with the house. The state says a freeze cannot pass to a later owner of the same home, and a buyer cannot claim the seller's earlier limitation.

The statute behind this is Ark. Code § 26-26-1123, which the Benton County assessor quotes. After a sale, the assessor values the property at 20% of its appraised value on the next assessment date following the transfer of title. The new owner cannot claim an assessment limitation until the second assessment date after the transfer. That is why a buyer's first tax bill can look sharply higher than the seller's last one.

Three steps are worth taking when you are the seller:

  • Tell the assessor when the house stops being your principal residence.
  • Do not expect a second credit. If you buy another home, the one-credit-per-year rule applies to you as an owner.
  • Settle at closing who pays the bill that arrives after the sale. Arkansas taxes are paid a year behind, so the 2026 assessment is billed in spring 2027 and due October 15, 2027, per the Benton County assessor.

Is the homestead tax credit the same as protection from creditors?

No. The tax credit lowers a property tax bill. Protection of a homestead from judgment creditors is a separate matter under Article 9 of the Arkansas Constitution.

An Arkansas court quoting Article 9, section 3 describes it this way: the homestead of a resident who is married or the head of a family is not subject to the lien of a judgment or to sale under execution, with exceptions the constitution lists. How that applies to a particular house, including one in bankruptcy, takes a lawyer's reading. Filing for the tax credit does not create or remove that protection.

How does the homestead credit fit into selling an Arkansas house for cash?

It matters most for the paperwork around the sale, since the credit ends with your ownership and the cash price does not change it.

Property taxes are due to the county collector by October 15 each year. Craighead County's collector says taxes unpaid after that date draw a 10% penalty, and Faulkner County's collector adds 10% annual interest on real estate taxes. Parcels that stay delinquent are certified to the Commissioner of State Lands, and title vests in the state, so a seller behind on taxes should clear the balance before listing or signing.

The deed carries its own tax. The Arkansas real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions above $100, as the Department of Finance and Administration states, paid through a stamp on the deed.

More questions about Arkansas Homestead Exemption

Does Arkansas have a homestead exemption?

Arkansas offers a homestead property tax credit rather than an exemption of value. It is worth up to $675 a year on a principal residence, and owners 65 or older or disabled can also apply to freeze the taxable assessed value.

Where do I apply for the Arkansas homestead credit?

You apply with the county assessor's office in the county where the home sits. The Department of Finance and Administration says the assessor handles both the credit and the age 65 or disability freeze, so ask that office for the form and the filing window.

Does the buyer inherit my homestead credit when I sell?

No. The buyer must apply as a new owner. Under Ark. Code § 26-26-1123 the buyer cannot claim a limit on assessed value until the second assessment date after the transfer, and a freeze cannot pass to a later owner.

Can I claim the credit on a rental or second home?

No. The credit applies only to a homestead used as the owner's principal place of residence, and an owner may claim only one credit per year.

Will turning 65 stop my property taxes from rising?

No. The freeze holds the taxable assessed value, not the bill. If a city, county or school district raises its millage rate, your taxes can still go up.

Can a trust or an LLC get the credit?

A trust can, because the home may be held in a revocable or irrevocable trust. An LLC can too when it files a certificate of good standing and a signed member attestation that the house is that member's primary residence.

Arkansas Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in Arkansas?

Get My Cash Offer →

Does Arkansas charge an estate tax when someone dies?

No. The Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration says the state estate tax was repealed by Act 645 of 2003, and that no Arkansas estate tax return is required for anyone who died after December 31, 2004.

For an heir holding a house, that settles the first worry. The state does not take a share of the estate based on its size, and there is no Arkansas return to file for the estate tax itself. DFA's one-page notice, revised in December 2020, is the source for this, and it is worth printing for the probate file if a title company or lender asks.

The notice speaks only to the estate tax. We could not open an official Arkansas page that addresses a separate inheritance tax, so this guide does not make a claim either way. An heir with a large inheritance can ask DFA or a probate attorney to confirm before distribution.

What about the federal estate tax?

The federal tax reaches only very large estates. The IRS states that a return is required when the gross estate, plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, is above the filing threshold for the year of death, and that threshold is $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

The IRS adds that most relatively simple estates do not need to file. When one does, the IRS says the gross estate is valued at fair market value on the date of death, and deductions can include mortgages and other debts, estate administration expenses, property that passes to a surviving spouse and qualified charities. A surviving spouse may also elect to carry over the decedent's unused exemption, known as portability, on a timely filed return.

Year of deathFederal filing thresholdArkansas estate tax return
2023$12,920,000None required
2024$13,610,000None required
2025$13,990,000None required
2026$15,000,000None required

Figures come from the IRS estate tax page and DFA's repeal notice.

What income tax can an heir owe on selling an inherited Arkansas house?

Often very little, because the heir's basis usually starts at the home's value when the owner died. IRS Publication 551 lists the fair market value on the date of death as the basis of inherited property, or the value on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative elects it. It adds that heirs who receive a Schedule A (Form 8971) generally use the estate tax value reported there.

Gain is measured from that starting figure to the sale price. If the house sells for about its date-of-death value, the taxable gain tends to be small. If it rises in value while the heir waits, the increase is the gain. Arkansas then taxes only half of a net long-term gain, as explained in our guide to Arkansas capital gains tax on a house sale.

Income earned by the estate itself, such as rent collected before the sale, is a separate matter. DFA keeps a page of fiduciary and estate income tax forms for personal representatives.

When can an Arkansas heir skip formal probate?

When the estate is small. Ark. Code 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and distribute estate assets without a personal representative if the property owned at death, less encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000. The decedent's homestead and any statutory allowances for a surviving spouse or minor children are left out of that count.

That exclusion helps with houses. A family home that was the decedent's homestead does not eat into the $100,000 limit, though it still appears in the affidavit.

  • At least 45 days must have passed since the death.
  • No petition for appointment of a personal representative can be pending or granted.
  • One or more distributees file an affidavit with the probate clerk of the circuit court in the proper county.
  • The affidavit states that there are no unpaid claims, and that the Department of Human Services either furnished no benefits or has been reimbursed.
  • It lists personal property with values, and real property by legal description with value, including the homestead.
  • The clerk charges $25 to file and $5 per certified copy, and no extra fee applies if a will is attached.

What extra steps apply when the small estate includes real property?

The distributee must publish a notice of the death and the affidavit within 30 days after filing. The notice gives creditors three months from the first publication to present verified claims, and late claims are barred.

That three-month window is the practical timeline for an heir who wants to sell. A buyer or title company may want to see that the affidavit was filed, the notice ran and the claims period passed before a deed is signed. The statute also allows the distributee to open a bank account in the estate's name without a petition or court order, which is handy for holding sale proceeds and paying the last bills.

Estates over the limit, or with a dispute among heirs, go through a regular administration in the circuit court's probate division. That route has its own filings, and a probate attorney can explain which one fits.

What costs come with transferring or selling the house?

The main closing cost the state adds is the real property transfer tax. DFA says it is $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on a deed or instrument conveying realty, on transactions over $100. Ark. Code 26-60-105 splits it into $1.10 per $1,000 and an added $2.20 per $1,000 that the statute says the purchaser pays.

Property tax is the other bill that follows the house. Under Ark. Code 26-36-201, real property tax is payable to the county collector from the first business day of March through October 15, taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent, and a 10% penalty applies. An estate that is still settling in the fall should check that the current year's bill has not slipped.

Utilities, insurance and upkeep continue until the deed is recorded, so a vacant inherited house can run up costs even when no tax is due on the estate.

What should heirs do first with an inherited Arkansas house?

Start by confirming who legally owns it and what has to be filed, then decide whether to keep, rent or sell.

  • Locate the will, the deed and the latest property tax statement.
  • Ask the county assessor or collector for the parcel's tax status.
  • Check whether the estate qualifies for the small estate affidavit, or needs a personal representative.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing, since it sets the basis for any later sale.
  • Secure the house and keep insurance active.
  • Speak with a probate attorney and a tax professional before signing a sale contract.

Heirs who live out of state, or who inherited a house needing repairs, sometimes choose a cash sale to avoid carrying costs and repair projects. The right choice depends on the estate's papers and the family's timeline.

More questions about Arkansas Estate and Inheritance Tax

Is there an Arkansas estate tax?

No. DFA says Act 645 of 2003 repealed the Arkansas estate tax, and no estate tax return is required for decedents who died after December 31, 2004.

Do heirs pay Arkansas inheritance tax on a house?

We could not confirm an Arkansas inheritance tax from an official page, so we make no claim. Ask DFA or a probate attorney, who can answer for your situation.

At what size does the federal estate tax apply?

A federal return is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption exceeds the filing threshold for the year of death. The IRS lists it as $15,000,000 for 2026.

What is the Arkansas small estate limit?

Under Ark. Code 28-41-101, property owned at death, less encumbrances, can be up to $100,000, not counting the homestead and statutory allowances for a surviving spouse or minor children. At least 45 days must pass after death.

How long do creditors have if real property is in a small estate?

Three months from the first publication of the notice. The notice must be published within 30 days after the affidavit is filed, and claims not presented in time are barred.

Will I owe tax if I sell an inherited house right away?

Usually little, since the basis is the fair market value at the date of death, per IRS Publication 551. The gain is the sale price minus that figure, and Arkansas taxes half of a net long-term gain.

What the official sources say

  • Failure to pay rent, or to pay on time, is grounds for eviction; a landlord may bring a civil 'unlawful detainer' action. (Landlord And Tenant Rights | Arkansas AG; source)
  • After receiving a summons, the tenant has five days to object in writing to the clerk; without an objection the sheriff can remove the tenant, and with one a hearing is scheduled. (Landlord And Tenant Rights | Arkansas AG; source)
  • Property left in the dwelling at lease termination is considered abandoned and may be disposed of by the landlord. (Landlord And Tenant Rights | Arkansas AG; source)

How does an eviction work in Arkansas?

Arkansas gives a landlord three separate ways to get a tenant out: a civil lawsuit called unlawful detainer, a case under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act of 2007, and a criminal charge for refusing to leave. Most owners start with one of the first two.

Unlawful detainer is defined in Ark. Code § 18-60-304. A person commits it by holding over after a lease ends, by refusing a written demand to leave, by failing to pay rent and then refusing to quit after three days' written notice, by letting the premises become unsafe or unhealthy, or by allowing a common nuisance. Legal Aid of Arkansas describes it as the most common type of eviction in the state.

The Landlord-Tenant Act route starts at § 18-17-901. A landlord or agent may file in district court when rent is not paid when due or demanded, when the term of occupancy has ended, or when the rental agreement has been broken. For a residential lease, rent that stays unpaid five days after the due date counts as legal notice that eviction proceedings can begin.

What notice periods apply to an Arkansas eviction?

The notice a landlord must give depends on the reason for ending the tenancy. The table lists each trigger found in the statutes and the state guidance.

SituationNotice or waiting periodWhere it comes from
Rent unpaid, unlawful detainerThree days' written notice to quit§ 18-60-304(3); Attorney General
Rent unpaid, Landlord-Tenant ActLandlord may terminate if rent is not paid within five days of the due date§ 18-17-701(b)
Other lease violationWritten notice with a termination date at least 14 days after receipt, if not fixed§ 18-17-701(a)
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice at least 7 days before the end date§ 18-17-704(a)
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice at least 30 days before the end date§ 18-17-704(b)
Criminal failure to vacateTen days' written notice to vacate§ 18-16-101(b)

Legal Aid of Arkansas summarizes the civil timing as at least three days for unpaid rent, at least 14 days for other violations, and at least one month to end a month-to-month tenancy. The Attorney General adds that a landlord may end a lease for any reason, giving one rental period's notice on an oral lease or notice under the terms of a written one.

The sources word these periods a little differently, so a landlord should match the notice to the lease and the statute that fits the facts.

What happens after the notice period ends?

If the tenant is still in the house, the landlord files a complaint with the court, and the case moves through a short series of steps.

  • Service. Legal Aid says the tenant must receive the summons and complaint through a process server or by certified mail.
  • Five days to object. The Attorney General says a tenant who receives a summons has five days to object in writing to the court clerk. Without an objection, the county sheriff can remove the tenant.
  • Order to vacate or show cause. Under the Landlord-Tenant Act, if the complaint carries an affidavit from someone with knowledge of the reason for eviction, the court issues an order to vacate or to appear and show cause within ten calendar days after service. A written answer counts as an appearance.
  • Hearing. If the tenant appears, the judge hears both sides. A judgment for the tenant lets the tenant stay until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, rent goes unpaid, or another eviction case succeeds (§ 18-17-908).
  • Writ of possession. If the landlord wins, the clerk issues a writ and the sheriff serves it. Legal Aid says the tenant then has 24 hours to leave. The sheriff carries out the writ under the procedure in § 18-60-310, as § 18-17-913 directs.

Each of these steps is a minimum. Court calendars set the hearing date, so no statute gives a fixed total number of days from notice to move-out.

What is the criminal failure to vacate charge?

It is a misdemeanor for a tenant who willfully refuses to leave after ten days' written notice from the landlord, the landlord's agent or the landlord's attorney. The rule is in Ark. Code § 18-16-101.

The same section says a renter who fails to pay rent when due forfeits the right to keep occupying the dwelling. On conviction the fine is between $1 and $25 per offense, and each day of willful holding over after the notice expires counts as a separate offense.

Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities?

No. Legal Aid of Arkansas states that a landlord needs a court order and a writ of possession carried out by the sheriff, and may not use self-help methods.

  • Changing the locks is a self-help eviction.
  • Removing the tenant's belongings, doors or windows is also self-help.
  • Shutting off water, power or other utilities is self-help as well.

Legal Aid adds an exception: the same acts may be lawful when the tenant has already moved out or the landlord reasonably believes the property is abandoned. A tenant who is locked out can sue for forcible entry, and the court may restore access and award damages, costs and attorney's fees. The landlord may counterclaim to evict in the same case, since a lockout alone does not give the tenant a right to stay when there is a legal ground for eviction.

What happens to belongings left in the house?

When a lease ends, voluntarily or not, the Attorney General says everything the tenant leaves behind is considered abandoned and the landlord may dispose of it as the landlord sees fit, without recourse by the tenant. Property left on the premises is also subject to a landlord's lien for sums the tenant agreed to pay.

Legal Aid describes the other situation. If law enforcement has to carry out the eviction, items the tenant cannot take are removed and stored at the tenant's expense. If the tenant moves out first and leaves things behind, the landlord can treat them as abandoned and throw them away or sell them.

Can a tenant withhold rent over repairs?

No. Section 18-17-502 says a tenant may not offset or withhold rent for an alleged or actual violation of the implied quality standards, and nothing in the chapter excuses a tenant from paying rent.

For leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, the statute implies several basics: hot and cold running water, electricity, potable water, working sanitary sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning if the home had them when the lease was signed. If the unit falls short, the tenant sends written notice. When rent is current and the landlord does not fix the problem within 30 calendar days, the tenant's sole remedy is to end the lease without penalty and receive back any recoverable security deposit.

The City of Little Rock adds its own minimum housing standards for privately owned rentals with two or more dwellings, including a safe roof that does not leak. Problems can be reported to the Department of Housing and Neighborhood Programs at 500 West Markham Street, Suite 120W, or (501) 371-6825.

What money can a landlord recover in an eviction?

A landlord can recover actual damages, obtain injunctive relief and get a judgment or eviction in circuit or district court without posting bond, according to § 18-17-701(c).

Attorney's fees are possible when the landlord is represented by a lawyer. They are available if nonpayment of rent is not in good faith, and for other willful noncompliance. On a holdover, § 18-17-704 allows fees when the tenant is not holding over in good faith. A willful violation can add up to three months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater.

How does an eviction affect selling a rented house in Arkansas?

The sale and the eviction are two separate tracks. The statutes above control who has the right to possession. They do not say that a sale ends a tenancy, so the lease terms and a lawyer's advice should come before any promise to a buyer that the house will be vacant.

A few practical points tie the two together. A landlord may decline to renew a lease for any reason except discriminatory ones covered by the Fair Housing Act, according to Legal Aid. A month-to-month tenant must be given 30 days' written notice. A buyer who is purchasing a house for cash can be asked whether it will take the property with the tenant still inside, which avoids waiting on a court calendar.

Tax paperwork follows the sale too. The Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration says the real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions above $100, shown on the deed through a transfer stamp. The Assessment Coordination Division also asks owners to tell the assessor when a house changes from owner-occupied to rental, which matters because the homestead credit only applies to a principal residence.

More questions about Arkansas Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does an Arkansas eviction take?

The statutes set minimum waits and no fixed total. Notice runs from three days to 30 days, a tenant has five days to object, a show-cause order allows up to ten days to appear, and a tenant served with a writ has 24 hours according to Legal Aid. A contested case adds a hearing date set by the court.

Is eviction a crime in Arkansas?

Only the failure to vacate charge is criminal. Under § 18-16-101, a tenant who willfully stays after ten days' written notice commits a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $1 to $25 per offense, and each day counts separately.

Can a landlord evict without going to court?

No. Legal Aid of Arkansas says a landlord needs a court order, and the sheriff carries out the writ of possession. Changing locks, removing doors or windows, or cutting utilities are illegal self-help methods unless the tenant has left or the property is reasonably believed abandoned.

Does a pending eviction stop me from selling the house?

Nothing in the statutes cited here bars a sale while a case is open. The lease and the buyer's terms decide what happens to the tenant, so ask an Arkansas attorney before you sign a contract that promises vacant possession.

Where can a tenant find free legal help with an eviction?

Legal Aid of Arkansas offers free help to tenants who qualify, and its number is 1-800-952-9243.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Quitclaim deeds given between divorcing parties as a division of marital property are exempt from the transfer tax. (26 CAR 166-102; source)
  • A quitclaim deed to a lienholder given to avoid foreclosure is exempt from the transfer tax. (26 CAR 166-102; source)
  • The Circuit Clerk acts as ex-officio recorder and serves as the Land Recorder for the county (Greene County example). (Circuit Clerk | Greene County; source)
  • DFA sells real estate transfer stamps and publishes an Affidavit of Compliance form for the transfer tax. (Real Property Transfer Tax | DFA; source)

What does a quitclaim deed do in Arkansas?

A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the signer has in the property and makes no promise that the interest is good. It does not clear a mortgage, a tax lien or a co-owner's share, so it works best between people who already trust the title.

Arkansas law treats the paper itself with care. A conveyance has to be acknowledged, the county recorder must accept the format, and a married owner's homestead brings the spouse into the signing. Each of those steps is spelled out in the sections below, with the statute behind it.

What must a deed look like for the recorder to accept it?

The recorder can refuse a deed that fails the format rules in Ark. Code 14-15-402. Missing a margin is the sort of slip that gets a deed sent back.

  • Paper size is 8.5 by 11 inches.
  • The first page needs 2.5 inches of blank space at the top right for the file mark.
  • Sides and bottom need 0.5 inch, and the last page needs 2.5 inches at the bottom.
  • The document carries its title and the names of grantor and grantee.
  • It must be legible and acknowledged under 16-47-207.

The recorder may waive the format for good cause. Documents signed before January 1, 2004, and plats and surveys, are exempt from the format rules.

A separate rule, 14-15-403, requires the preparer's name and address on the first page of an instrument that affects title. A recorder who accepts a noncompliant instrument must refund the fee on request within six months, and the instrument still gives notice. Wills, court decrees and instruments signed before August 1, 1959 are exempt.

Does a spouse have to sign a quitclaim on a homestead?

Yes, when the property is the homestead of a married person, the spouse must join in the deed or sign a separate deed and acknowledge it. Ark. Code 18-12-403 says an instrument affecting a married person's homestead has no validity without that participation.

The exceptions are taxes, laborers' and mechanics' liens, and purchase money. Under 18-12-202, a married person may acknowledge a conveyance of their own property, or release dower, curtesy or homestead in a spouse's property, as if unmarried, with no separate examination.

A quitclaim signed by one spouse alone can leave a gap in the title. If the house was a homestead, ask the title company whether the other spouse's signature is needed.

What if the acknowledgment has a mistake?

Some acknowledgment defects are cured once the deed is recorded, but the cure should not be treated as a plan. Section 18-12-208 lists defects that do not defeat a recorded instrument.

  • A missing or wrong notary seal, for deeds signed after August 13, 1993.
  • A missing or wrong commission expiration date.
  • A wrong date or a missing county.
  • A notary who moved out of the commissioning county.
  • Wording that departs from the statutory form but makes a good-faith attempt at material compliance.

A defective but recorded deed still gives constructive notice of its contents. For instruments recorded on or after April 8, 2013, a proper jurat can substitute for an acknowledgment certificate.

What does recording and transfer tax cost?

Recording fees are set by statute and charged by the circuit clerk, who serves as recorder. Pulaski County's published schedule shows $15 for the first page of a deed and $5 for each added page, under Ark. Code 21-6-306. Other counties post their own schedules, so ask the clerk where the land sits.

ItemAmountSource
Deed, first page (Pulaski County)$15.00Pulaski County Clerk fee schedule
Each added page$5.00Pulaski County Clerk fee schedule
Document non-compliance fee$25.00 per document, plus page feesPulaski County Clerk fee schedule
State transfer tax, base$1.10 per $1,000Ark. Code 26-60-105(a)
State transfer tax, added$2.20 per $1,000, paid by purchaserArk. Code 26-60-105(b)

The two tax pieces add to $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration, and the tax applies only when consideration is over $100, according to the state revenue division. The Miscellaneous Tax Section sells the transfer stamps and can be reached at 501-682-7187.

Which quitclaim deeds are exempt from the transfer tax?

Several transfers are exempt, and a family quitclaim may fall under one of them. Section 26-60-102 lists twelve categories, including these.

  • Property divided between divorcing parties.
  • Instruments given only to secure a debt, and certain transfers to a secured party enforcing a security interest.
  • Corrections of a recorded instrument when tax was already paid.
  • Land sold for delinquent taxes.
  • Beneficiary deeds under 18-12-608.
  • Transfers to or from governments, and some business entity reorganizations.

A FHA, VA or USDA Rural Development home is exempt if the price is $60,000 or less and the seller files a sworn statement that the buyer and spouse have owned no home in the prior three years. A gift between relatives does not appear among the categories, so confirm with the state revenue office before assuming an exemption.

Is a beneficiary deed a better tool than a quitclaim?

For passing a house at death, a beneficiary deed can be the cleaner choice, because it does nothing until the owner dies. Ark. Code 18-12-608 sets the terms: it must say it is not effective until death, and it is valid only if recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

  • The owner can revoke it at any time by a signed, recorded revocation. A will cannot revoke it.
  • If several deeds exist, the last one signed before death controls, whatever the recording order.
  • The transfer remains subject to mortgages, liens and leases that exist at death.
  • For joint tenants or spouses holding by the entirety, the deed must be signed by all surviving owners.

The deed is also exempt from the transfer tax. A quitclaim to a child during life hands over a present interest, so speak with a lawyer before choosing between the two.

What is a sensible order of steps for a quitclaim?

Work through the checks in the order the statutes create them, so the recorder has nothing to reject.

  • Confirm every owner and whether the house is a married person's homestead.
  • Put the preparer's name and address on the first page, and leave the file-mark space at the top right.
  • Sign before a notary, with the acknowledgment naming the state and county.
  • Check whether the transfer falls under an exemption, and buy transfer stamps if it does not.
  • Record the deed with the county recorder where the property is located, and keep the receipt.

When does a quitclaim get in the way of selling?

A quitclaim can slow a sale if the buyer's title company questions the gap it creates. Common trouble spots are a missing spouse signature, a mortgage still in the old owner's name, and unpaid property tax.

The tax lien binds the house and ranks ahead of other liens, per 26-34-101, so a deed between family does not move the tax debt away. Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses, including houses where a quitclaim was recorded. If a quitclaim is already recorded on your house, have the recorded copy and any mortgage statement ready when you call.

More questions about Arkansas Quitclaim Deed

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. It passes only the interest the signer holds and makes no promise about liens, co-owners or defects. A mortgage or tax lien stays on the property after a quitclaim.

Does my spouse have to sign if I quitclaim our home?

Yes, if it is your homestead. Section 18-12-403 makes a homestead instrument invalid unless the spouse joins or signs a separate acknowledged deed, with exceptions for taxes, certain liens and purchase money.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Arkansas?

Pulaski County charges $15 for the first page and $5 for each additional page. Other counties publish their own schedules, so check with the circuit clerk in the county where the land is.

What is the Arkansas real estate transfer tax rate?

It is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transfers above $100: $1.10 base plus $2.20 paid by the purchaser. Divorce divisions, security deeds and beneficiary deeds are among the exemptions.

Can I use a quitclaim to transfer a house to my child at death?

A beneficiary deed under 18-12-608 is built for that. It must state it takes effect at death and be recorded before the owner dies.

What if the recorder rejects my deed?

The format rules in 14-15-402 and the preparer statement in 14-15-403 are the usual causes. Fix the margins, names or preparer information and resubmit, or ask the recorder about a good-cause waiver, which may carry a $25 fee.

What the official sources say

  • No legal or equitable interest vests in the grantee until the owner's death prior to revocation. (Act 570 of 2021; source)
  • The transfer is subject to existing encumbrances and to a DHS claim for reimbursement of federal or state benefits from the estate or the interest acquired by the grantee (under 20-76-436). (Act 570 of 2021; source)

Arkansas Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Arkansas rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Arkansas?

Arkansas calls it a beneficiary deed. Ark. Code 18-12-608 defines it as a deed, given without current tangible consideration, that conveys an ownership interest to a named grantee when the owner dies, and the deed must say in express terms that it does not take effect until that death.

People search for the same thing under several names (TOD deed, transfer on death deed, beneficiary deed), but the rules live in one code section. The legislature built that section in layers: Act 1918 of 2005, Act 243 of 2007 and Act 570 of 2021.

While the owner is alive, the grantee holds nothing. Subsection (a)(1)(B) says no legal or equitable interest vests in the grantee until the owner dies without having revoked the deed. That one sentence explains most of the rest. The owner keeps control of the house, and the person named has no interest to sell, pledge or claim during the owner's life.

What must the deed contain to be valid?

A valid Arkansas beneficiary deed names the grantee, states that it takes effect only at death, and is recorded before the owner dies. The recording step is the one that most often decides whether the deed works at all.

  • An express statement that the deed has no effect until the owner's death (subsection (a)(1)(A)).
  • A designated grantee, or several, with the form of co-ownership stated.
  • Recording in the county recorder's office of the county where the property sits, before the owner's death. Under (c)(1), a deed not recorded in time is not valid.
  • For property held as tenants by the entirety or as joint tenants with survivorship, a deed designated by all surviving owners that takes effect at the death of the last survivor (b)(1).
  • Substantial compliance with the statutory form, which the code links to rather than reproducing in the text (g).

If fewer than all owners sign, subsection (b)(2) says the deed is valid only when the last surviving owner was one of the signers. Subsection (f)(2) separately says the section does not invalidate a deed that is otherwise effective by law and is recorded only after death, which refers to other kinds of deeds, not to a beneficiary deed.

Where does each rule sit in section 18-12-608?

The table below maps the main subsections of the 2025 code text as published on Justia. Use it to find the exact language before you rely on a summary, including this one.

SubsectionWhat it covers
(a)(1)Definition, effect at death, no vesting before death, transfer subject to encumbrances made before or after the deed
(a)(2) and (a)(3)More than one grantee, and successor grantees
(b)Entireties and survivorship property, deeds signed by fewer than all owners
(c)Recording before death, and transfers to a trustee
(d)Revocation, and no revocation by will
(e)Several deeds for one property
(f)Other lawful ways to delay an interest until death
(g) and (h)Statutory forms for the deed and for a revocation

Who can be named as grantee?

The owner can name one person, several people, a successor, or a trustee. The statute is flexible on all four.

  • Several grantees may hold as joint tenants with survivorship, tenants in common, tenants by the entirety, or under any other valid tenancy (a)(2).
  • A successor grantee can be named, including the unnamed heirs of the first grantee, if the deed states the condition that triggers the successor, such as the first grantee not surviving the owner (a)(3).
  • The deed can pass the property to a trustee, including the trustee of a revocable trust, and can name unnamed successor trustees (c)(2).

How the grantees hold title matters later, when the house is sold. A title company will want to know who has to sign, so the tenancy language in the deed is worth reading closely before anyone lists the property.

How do you revoke or replace a beneficiary deed?

The owner may revoke at any time before death by recording a revocation in the same county recorder's office. Subsection (d)(2) requires the revocation to be both executed and recorded while the owner is alive.

Where several owners signed the original deed, any signing owner may revoke. If fewer than all owners sign the revocation, (d)(3) makes it effective only if the last surviving owner signed it and recorded it before that owner's death.

A will cannot undo the deed. Under (d)(4), a compliant beneficiary deed cannot be revoked, altered or amended by the owner's will. If an owner signs more than one beneficiary deed for the same property, subsection (e) gives effect to the one signed last before death, whatever order they were recorded in.

Can the state recover Medicaid costs from a house passed by beneficiary deed?

Yes, it can. Act 570 of 2021 added language to 18-12-608(a)(1)(B) making the transfer subject to a Department of Human Services claim for reimbursement of federal or state benefits, and it amended section 20-76-436 so the department may claim against the interest a grantee acquires, not only against the estate.

The department's own estate recovery guide describes who is exposed and who is not.

  • People age 55 or older who received long-term care Medicaid in a nursing home or through a home and community-based waiver are covered. Under 55, only people permanently institutionalized.
  • The claim is limited to what Medicaid paid for long-term care, and heirs are not liable above the value of the estate.
  • No claim is made while a surviving spouse is alive, while a child is under 21, or for a blind or disabled child under the guide's conditions.
  • A hardship waiver committee can waive the claim. Factors include whether the home is the sole income-producing asset and whether the home is worth 50 percent or less of the average home price in the county.

Act 570 also gives a grantee a way to ask. If the grantee requests a release or disclaimer in writing, the department has 30 calendar days to either assert a claim or provide a disclaimer and release suitable for recording. Without probate, the guide says the department sends a demand notice to the county clerk's office and acts if the home is sold.

Does a beneficiary deed replace every other estate step?

No. The deed moves only the real property it describes. Bank accounts, vehicles and other assets still follow a will, beneficiary designations or the small estate procedure.

For small estates, section 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and distribute property by affidavit, filed with the probate clerk in the right county. The clerk charges $25 to file and $5 per certified copy. The affidavit has to say whether the Department of Human Services provided benefits and, if it did, that the department has been reimbursed.

When the estate includes real property, the distributee must publish notice of the death and the affidavit within 30 days of filing, and creditors then have three months from first publication to present claims. That publication step is one reason families sometimes prefer a recorded beneficiary deed for the house itself.

What does a grantee face when selling an inherited Arkansas house?

A grantee who wants to sell first needs the recorded deed, the owner's death record and any department notice lined up, then a buyer and a closing. The sale itself carries the usual real estate transfer tax: $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100, paid by buying a transfer stamp, according to the Department of Finance and Administration. The Miscellaneous Tax Section at 501-682-7187 handles corrections to a stamp.

Practical points to settle before listing:

  • Whether any mortgage or lien survives, since the transfer is subject to encumbrances made before or after the deed.
  • Whether the department has sent a claim or a demand notice.
  • Whether the deed named several grantees and how they hold title.
  • Whether the house needs repairs a traditional buyer's lender would require.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands once the title questions are answered. This page is general information, so an Arkansas attorney or title company should confirm the steps for your deed.

More questions about Arkansas Transfer on Death Deed

Does an Arkansas beneficiary deed avoid probate?

It moves the named interest at death under the statute's own terms, so the house does not pass under the owner's will. The transfer is still subject to encumbrances and to a possible Department of Human Services claim, and other assets may still need a probate or small estate step.

When must the deed be recorded?

Before the owner dies. Subsection (c)(1) of 18-12-608 requires recording in the county recorder's office where the property is located, and a deed not recorded in time is not valid.

Can an owner change their mind after recording?

Yes. The owner can record a revocation at any time before death, or sign a newer beneficiary deed. If there are several deeds, the one signed last before death is effective, even if another was recorded later.

Can a will cancel a beneficiary deed?

No. Subsection (d)(4) says a compliant beneficiary deed cannot be revoked, altered or amended by the owner's will.

Does the grantee have to sign or accept the deed?

The text of subsections (a) through (h) of 18-12-608 does not require acceptance by the grantee. The owner signs and records the deed, and the grantee's interest vests only at the owner's death if the deed has not been revoked.

Which county court handles an Arkansas probate?

Probate is filed in the circuit court of the county where the dead person lived. Under Ark. Code 28-40-102, a nonresident's estate goes to the county that holds most of the in-state property by value, and someone who died in Arkansas with no home or property here is handled where the death occurred.

Arkansas has 75 counties, so the clerk you deal with depends on where the house sits and where the owner lived. If cases start in two counties, the later one is stayed until the circuit court in the first county decides venue. A judge may also transfer a case before final distribution when it was filed in the wrong county or a move helps the estate.

For a seller this matters because a house in Garland County can belong to an estate opened in Pulaski County. The county recorder where the land lies still records the deeds. The probate court and the recorder are different offices.

Who is allowed to run the estate?

The person named as executor in the will has first claim, followed by the surviving spouse, then other people who share in the estate. Section 28-48-101 sets the order and puts a short clock on some of it.

  • A surviving spouse, or the spouse's nominee, petitions within 30 days after the death.
  • Other people entitled to a share, or their nominee, apply within 40 days if there is a spouse and within 30 days if there is none.
  • Anyone else who is qualified can apply after that.

A person under 18, a person of unsound mind, an unpardoned felon, a corporation not authorized to act as a fiduciary in Arkansas, and anyone the court finds unsuitable are disqualified. A nonresident can serve only if an agent is appointed to accept papers, and that agent may be the court clerk. Heirs who live out of state should check this rule before they plan to serve.

Who owns the house the moment the owner dies?

If there is no will, the real estate passes to the heirs immediately, while personal property goes to the personal representative. The Arkansas courts' probate benchbook points to Ark. Code 28-9-203 for that rule, and to 28-9-206 for the limits on it.

Those limits are the surviving spouse's dower or curtesy, the homestead rights of the spouse and children, and the statutory allowances for a spouse and minor children. A spouse married to the decedent for more than a year can also elect against a will. The benchbook adds that where there are no descendants the spouse takes the estate, and a marriage of under three years cuts the spouse's share to 50%.

So an heir can hold title on paper and still be unable to deliver a clean sale. A buyer, a title company or a lender will want to see who the heirs are and whether the court has appointed anyone. Spouse and child homestead rights can reduce what an heir is free to sell.

When can a small estate skip a formal case?

An heir, called a distributee, can collect a small estate with an affidavit when no petition for a personal representative is pending, 45 days have passed, and the net estate is $100,000 or less, with the homestead and spousal and child allowances left out of that count. These terms come from Ark. Code 28-41-101.

The affidavit goes to the probate clerk in the proper county. It must give a legal description and value for any real property, name who lives there, and list the people entitled to receive it. It must also say there are no unpaid claims and that any Department of Human Services benefits were reimbursed. The clerk's fee is $25 to file and $5 per certified copy, and attaching a will adds no fee.

When real estate is involved, the distributee publishes notice of the death and the filing within 30 days. Creditors then have three months from first publication to present verified claims. The statute lists what the affidavit contains and the publication step. It does not spell out how the affidavit changes title to land, so a seller should ask the title company what it will accept before relying on it.

How long do creditors have to come forward?

In a formal administration, creditors generally have six months from the first published notice. Section 28-50-101 bars late claims, with a few timing rules layered on top.

ItemPeriod
Standard claim deadline6 months after first publication
Copy of notice to known heirs and creditorsWithin 1 month after first publication
Extra time if a creditor is served late30 more days after the period ends
Known creditors who never got noticeBarred 2 years after first publication
Outer limit if no letters or notice5 years after death
Small estate affidavit, real property3 months from first publication

Mortgages and other liens on estate property are not affected by the claims deadline. A lender holding a mortgage on the house keeps its lien even after the six months pass, so the payoff still comes out of any sale.

How does a personal representative sell estate real estate?

When the representative sells land, the court's order sets the terms, and an appraisal comes first. The rules sit in 28-51-302 and 28-51-303.

  • Three disinterested appraisers who know local values appraise the property under oath, though the court may approve a single appraiser if no heir or beneficiary objects.
  • The appraisal is filed with the clerk before the court issues the sale order.
  • The order states whether the sale is private or by auction, and whether it is for cash or on payment terms.
  • A private sale must bring at least the full appraised value. An auction must bring at least three-fourths of it.
  • A sale cannot close more than six months after the order unless the court-ordered reappraisal happened within the 30 days before the sale.

Because of these floors, an offer on a probate house has to be measured against the appraisal. An as-is offer from a cash buyer has to be measured against that appraisal and the hearing schedule.

How long can a will wait before it is filed?

An application to probate a will must be made within five years of the death, under Ark. Code 28-40-103. The limit has exceptions for fraudulent concealment of a will and for a nonresident's will already probated elsewhere.

For a recorded purchase of Arkansas real property from a nonresident's estate, a late probate of the will does not harm the buyer. Families who let a house sit for years should know the clock exists, but waiting also lets taxes, insurance and repair bills pile up on a property nobody has authority over.

What do sellers of inherited houses in Arkansas usually run into?

The common problems are unclear authority, heirs in several states, a mortgage still in the decedent's name, and a house that has sat empty. Each one slows a sale in a different way.

  • No one has been appointed, so no one can sign for the estate.
  • The heirs disagree about keeping or selling, and all of them hold an interest in real estate that passes at death.
  • Property taxes keep coming. The tax lien takes priority over other liens, so unpaid bills follow the house.
  • A court-approved sale must meet the appraisal floor and a hearing date.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on inherited houses in Arkansas. Bring the court paperwork you have, and ask an Arkansas probate attorney which route fits your estate.

More questions about Arkansas Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do all Arkansas estates have to go through probate?

No. When no petition for a personal representative is pending, 45 days have passed and the net estate is $100,000 or less (not counting the homestead and family allowances), a distributee can use the small estate affidavit instead. Larger estates, and estates where authority is disputed, go through the circuit court.

How soon must a spouse ask to be named personal representative?

Within 30 days after the death, if the spouse wants priority over other heirs. Other people entitled to a share apply within 40 days when there is a surviving spouse and within 30 days when there is none, under Ark. Code 28-48-101.

Can heirs sell the house before the estate is closed?

Real estate passes to the heirs at death when there is no will, but spouse and child homestead rights still apply. A buyer and title company will usually want proof of who has authority, so most sales wait for an appointment or an accepted affidavit.

What price must a probate house bring?

If the court orders a private sale, the price must be at least the full appraised value. An auction must bring at least three-fourths of it. The sale cannot close later than six months after the order without a fresh court-ordered appraisal.

Does a mortgage disappear when the owner dies?

No. The claims deadline does not affect mortgages or other liens on estate property, so the lender keeps its lien and the balance is paid from sale proceeds.

Can you probate an old will years after the death?

Yes, up to five years after death under Ark. Code 28-40-103, with exceptions for concealed wills and nonresident wills. After that the application is generally too late.

What the official sources say

  • Arkansas taxes 50% of net long-term capital gain: the Arkansas taxable amount equals line 7b multiplied by 50 percent. (AR1000D Capital Gains 2024 | DFA; source)
  • Net capital loss deduction is limited to $3,000 ($1,500 per taxpayer for filing status 4 or 5). (AR1000D Capital Gains 2024 | DFA; source)
  • Short-term capital gains are included in full in Arkansas taxable capital gain. (AR1000D Capital Gains 2024 | DFA; source)

Does Arkansas tax the profit when you sell a house?

Yes, if the profit is not sheltered by the federal home sale exclusion. Arkansas starts from your federal capital gain figures and then applies its own discount, which means only part of a long-term gain ends up in Arkansas taxable income.

The Department of Finance and Administration explains the mechanics on its 2025 Form AR1000D. The form opens with the rule in one line: only 50% of the net long-term capital gain is taxed, and the other half is exempt from state tax. You complete it when you have a gain or loss on federal Schedule D, or a gain on Form 1040 when Schedule D is not required.

A house sale that is fully excluded at the federal level may never reach the form. A sale that produces a taxable federal gain does, and the Arkansas return picks it up from there.

How does the federal home sale exclusion affect an Arkansas sale?

It usually decides whether any gain is taxed at all. The IRS says a seller may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return, if both the ownership test and the use test are met.

Both tests look at the five years ending on the sale date. You need to have owned the home for at least 24 months and used it as a residence for at least 24 months, and those two periods do not have to be the same stretch of time. On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test but both must meet the use test. The IRS also says you generally cannot use the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home in the two years before this sale. The agency's Topic 701 and Publication 523 hold the exceptions.

Reporting is a separate duty. If you receive Form 1099-S, the IRS says you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable. Sellers who cannot exclude the whole gain report it on Schedule D and Form 8949.

  • Owned the home at least 24 months of the last 5 years: ownership test met.
  • Lived in it at least 24 months of the last 5 years: use test met.
  • No other home gain excluded in the prior two years: generally required.
  • Gain above $250,000 single or $500,000 joint: the excess is taxable.

Why was the old Arkansas exclusion for sellers over 55 repealed?

The legislature repealed it in 1997, and it no longer applies. Arkansas Code 26-51-305 once let a taxpayer who had reached 55 make a one-time election to exclude up to $125,000 of home sale gain, or $62,500 on a married separate return, if the home was the principal residence for three of the previous five years.

The Code of Arkansas Rules still carries that text at 26 CAR 100-116, marked repealed, with a note that Acts 1997, No. 328, section 8 removed the statute. A seller reading older retirement guides may see references to the election. It is gone, so Arkansas now leans on the federal exclusion and the 50% rule.

What is the Arkansas rate and how does the 50% rule work?

The top individual income tax rate is 3.9%, and half of a net long-term gain is taxed at the ordinary rates. DFA announced in July 2024 that the General Assembly and the governor had cut the top rate from 4.4% to 3.9%.

Here is the arithmetic on the form. A net long-term gain is entered on line 7a. Line 7b caps the amount at $10,000,000, and line 8 multiplies it by 50 percent. The result is the Arkansas taxable amount for long-term gains. As an illustration only, a $100,000 net long-term gain would put $50,000 into Arkansas taxable income, and your own tax depends on your total income and the rate schedule that applies to you.

The form also says the part of a net gain above ten million dollars, for gains realized on or after January 1, 2014, is exempt from state tax. That threshold is far above a typical house sale.

ItemArkansas treatmentSource
Net long-term gain50% taxedDFA Form AR1000D
Short-term gainIncluded in fullDFA Form AR1000D
Net gain above $10,000,000Exempt (gains realized on or after Jan. 1, 2014)DFA Form AR1000D
Net capital loss deduction$3,000 ($1,500 per taxpayer for filing status 4 or 5)DFA Form AR1000D
Top income tax rate3.9% after the 2024 cutDFA news release, July 15, 2024

What if I owned the house for less than a year?

A short-term gain is taxed differently. The form states that short-term gains are included in full in the Arkansas taxable capital gain, with no 50% reduction. Anyone who buys a house, fixes it and sells it within a year should plan around that.

Losses are limited. When your capital losses exceed your gains, the amount you can deduct against other income is $3,000, or $1,500 per taxpayer for filing status 4 or 5. The limit matters most to investors and landlords who sell a rental or a flip at a loss.

How do rental and investment houses differ?

Rental houses do not get the home sale exclusion unless the owner meets the residence tests, so more of the profit tends to be taxable. Arkansas also notes on Form AR1000D that it did not adopt the federal bonus depreciation provision from previous years. Depreciation claimed federally can therefore differ from the Arkansas amount, and lines 2, 5 and 10 of the form adjust for that difference.

For an owner of a rental, the practical steps are these:

  • Pull the federal depreciation schedule for each year of ownership.
  • Compare it with the amounts allowed on the Arkansas return.
  • Enter any difference on the AR1000D adjustment lines.
  • Confirm the result with a tax professional before filing.

Investors who sell on an installment contract, with part of the price paid in a later year, can use the IRS installment method. The IRS says the home exclusion remains available even if the installment method defers some gain.

How is an inherited house treated?

The basis usually resets to the home's value on the date the owner died, which often removes most of the gain. IRS Publication 551 lists the fair market value at the date of death as the basis for inherited property, or the fair market value on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative chooses it.

That matters to heirs who sell soon after probate. If the house is worth about what it was worth at death, the taxable gain on the sale may be small. If it appreciated afterward, the difference from the date-of-death value is the starting point. Arkansas has no estate or inheritance tax to add on top, and our companion guide on Arkansas estate and inheritance tax covers that.

What other taxes show up at an Arkansas closing?

The main one is the real property transfer tax. DFA says it applies to each deed or instrument conveying realty, at $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on transactions over $100. Ark. Code 26-60-105 splits it into $1.10 per $1,000 under subsection (a) and an additional $2.20 per $1,000 under subsection (b), the latter stated to be paid by the purchaser.

The tax is based only on the price paid for land and buildings. Under section 26-60-105(c), consideration for tangible or intangible personal property is left out when a conveyance includes both. On a $150,000 sale, $3.30 per $1,000 works out to $495 in total, before any exemption. DFA's Miscellaneous Tax Section at 501-682-7187 handles stamp questions and corrections.

Property tax on the house is a separate matter from this transfer tax. The county collector's office can supply the balance due on the parcel before closing.

More questions about Arkansas Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does Arkansas have a capital gains tax?

Arkansas does not have a separate capital gains tax. Gains are included in income tax, but only 50% of a net long-term gain is taxed, per DFA Form AR1000D, and short-term gains are included in full.

Is the sale of my home taxable in Arkansas?

Only if the gain is not excluded federally. The IRS excludes up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, or $500,000 on a joint return, when the ownership and use tests are met. Gain above those amounts flows to your Arkansas return.

Is there still an Arkansas exclusion for homeowners over 55?

No. The one-time $125,000 election in Ark. Code 26-51-305 was repealed by Acts 1997, No. 328, section 8.

What is the top Arkansas income tax rate?

It is 3.9%. DFA announced the cut from 4.4% to 3.9% in July 2024.

Which form do I file for a gain on a house sale?

Arkansas Form AR1000D is completed when you have a capital gain or loss reported on federal Schedule D, or a gain on Form 1040 when Schedule D is not required. Its result carries to your Arkansas return.

How much transfer tax is due when I sell?

The state real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions over $100, according to DFA. The statute states that the additional $2.20 per $1,000 is paid by the purchaser.
